items.title: About the framework
items.text:
Temporal-boost is a lightweight, high-level framework for rapid development of Temporal-based microservices in Python. Built on top of the official Temporal Python SDK, it provides a FastAPI-inspired developer experience that makes building Temporal applications faster and more intuitive.

If you're familiar with FastAPI's declarative style and want to build reliable, scalable workflows with Temporal, this framework is designed for you.

items.title: Why Temporal-boost?
items.text:
• FastAPI-style API: Organize your Temporal workers similar to how you organize FastAPI routes
  • Zero boilerplate: Focus on your business logic, not infrastructure setup
  • Operations: Built-in logging, tracing, and metrics; coordinated shutdown for managed workers
  • Flexible: Support for activities, workflows, CRON schedules, and ASGI apps
  • Type-safe: Full type hints and Pydantic integration support

items.title: Main dependencies
items.text:
• Temporal SDK (Python) - Core Temporal functionality
  • Pydantic - Data validation and serialization
  • Typer - Modern CLI interface
  • Python logging - Built-in structured logging configuration
  • ASGI servers - Hypercorn, Uvicorn, Granian for running web applications

items.title: Main features
items.text:
• ✅ FastAPI-style application with pluggable workers (like routers)
  • ✅ Centralized logging and tracing management
  • ✅ Simple CRON workflow support with declarative scheduling
  • ✅ ASGI integration for FastAPI, Starlette, or any ASGI application
  • ✅ FastStream integration for event-driven architectures
  • ✅ Environment-based configuration for all settings
  • ✅ Prometheus metrics support out of the box
  • ✅ Graceful shutdown for workers implementing the managed stop contract
  • ✅ CLI interface for running workers individually or together

items.title: Basic installation
items.text:
Install the core package:

pip install temporal-boost

or with uv:

uv add temporal-boost

items.title: Optional extras
items.text:
Install additional features as needed:

# FastStream integration for event-driven workers
pip install "temporal-boost[faststream]"

# ASGI server support (choose one or more)
pip install "temporal-boost[uvicorn]"      # Uvicorn ASGI server
pip install "temporal-boost[hypercorn]"    # Hypercorn ASGI server
pip install "temporal-boost[granian]"      # Granian ASGI server

# Install all extras
pip install "temporal-boost[faststream,uvicorn,hypercorn,granian]"

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Python >= 3.10
  • Access to a Temporal server (local or remote)

items.title: Your first Temporal-boost application
items.text:
Create a file main.py:

import logging
from datetime import timedelta
from temporalio import activity, workflow
from temporal_boost import BoostApp

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

# Create your BoostApp instance
app = BoostApp(name="my-first-app")

# Define an activity
@activity.defn(name="greet_activity")
async def greet_activity(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

# Define a workflow
@workflow.defn(sandboxed=False, name="GreetingWorkflow")
class GreetingWorkflow:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, name: str) -> str:
        return await workflow.execute_activity(
            greet_activity,
            name,
            task_queue="greeting_queue",
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(minutes=1),
        )

# Register workers
app.add_worker(
    "greeting_worker",
    "greeting_queue",
    activities=[greet_activity],
    workflows=[GreetingWorkflow],
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

items.text:

items.title: Running your application
items.text:

python3 main.py run all

Or run a specific worker:

python3 main.py run greeting_worker

items.title: Example: Execute a workflow
items.text:
Create a client script to start your workflow:

import asyncio
from temporalio.client import Client

async def main():
    client = await Client.connect("localhost:7233")

    result = await client.execute_workflow(
        "GreetingWorkflow",
        "World",
        id="greeting-workflow-1",
        task_queue="greeting_queue",
    )

    print(f"Workflow result: {result}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Run it:

python3 client.py
# Output: Workflow result: Hello, World!

items.text:
Configure Temporal runtime with custom telemetry and metrics:

from temporal_boost import BoostApp
from temporalio.runtime import LoggingConfig, PrometheusConfig, Runtime

app = BoostApp("advanced-app")

worker = app.add_worker("custom_worker", "custom_queue", activities=[...])

# Configure custom runtime
worker.configure_temporal_runtime(
    prometheus_bind_address="0.0.0.0:9090",
    prometheus_counters_total_suffix=True,
    prometheus_unit_suffix=True,
    prometheus_durations_as_seconds=True,
    global_tags={"environment": "production", "service": "my-service"},
    attach_service_name=True,
    metric_prefix="temporal_boost",
)

items.title: Worker Builder Pattern
items.text:
Use builders directly for explicit runtime ownership. The runnable example example_runtime.py contains this complete async lifecycle:

import asyncio

from temporalio import activity

from temporal_boost.temporal.client import TemporalClientBuilder
from temporal_boost.temporal.runtime import TemporalRuntimeBuilder
from temporal_boost.temporal.worker import TemporalWorkerBuilder


@activity.defn
async def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}!"


async def run_worker() -> None:
    runtime = TemporalRuntimeBuilder(prometheus_bind_address="127.0.0.1:9090").build()
    client_builder = TemporalClientBuilder(target_host="localhost:7233", namespace="default")
    client_builder.set_runtime(runtime)
    client = await client_builder.build()
    worker_builder = TemporalWorkerBuilder(task_queue="custom_queue")
    worker_builder.set_client(client)
    worker_builder.set_activities([greet])
    worker = worker_builder.build()
    async with worker:
        # Keep serving until cancelled; the context shuts down the SDK worker.
        await asyncio.Event().wait()

The caller keeps the runtime alive while its client and worker use it. The supported SDK has no public runtime close() method: after worker shutdown, release references to the worker, client, builders, and runtime. An external reference can keep its exporter alive. This standalone example creates one runtime; BoostApp workers each create their own runtime.

items.title: Metrics Across Workers and Processes
items.text:
The CLI no longer creates, validates, or changes PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR. Temporal SDK exporters do not consume the Python Prometheus client's multiprocess directory. If another part of your application uses that variable, your application owns its path, validation, and cleanup; the CLI leaves directories, regular files, missing paths, and the environment untouched. Upgrading removes the old automatic temporary directory allocation; configure and scrape SDK exporter endpoints explicitly as described below.

Each TemporalBoostWorker owns an independent SDK runtime and client. There is no automatic runtime sharing. A Prometheus exporter belongs to that runtime and binds its own listening socket. The supported topology is a distinct endpoint for every concurrently running worker runtime, scraped individually by Prometheus. SDK OpenTelemetryConfig can instead send each runtime's metrics to an external collector configured by your deployment.

Deployment Exporter endpoints to scrape Two workers in one process Two distinct addresses, for example :9100 and :9101 Two processes, each running two workers on one host Four distinct addresses, for example :9100 through :9103 Two pods/containers, each running two workers Both ports in each pod/container, for example pod-a:9100, pod-a:9101, pod-b:9100, pod-b:9101

Configure each worker before starting it or accessing temporal_client_runtime. This fragment assumes payments and notifications were returned by app.add_worker(...):

payments.configure_temporal_runtime(
    prometheus_bind_address="0.0.0.0:9100",
    global_tags={"boost_worker": "payments"},
)
notifications.configure_temporal_runtime(
    prometheus_bind_address="0.0.0.0:9101",
    global_tags={"boost_worker": "notifications"},
)

The default TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_BIND_ADDRESS is applied to each worker, so one fixed address is appropriate for a single runtime. Override it per worker when starting more than one. For processes sharing a network address, allocate separate port ranges. The external --workers N launcher repeats the application configuration; it does not allocate metrics ports or aggregate SDK metrics. Prefer separate processes with explicit port ranges, or pods with separate network addresses. Scrape each worker endpoint in every replica using static targets or service discovery.

The runnable metrics example has two workers. With a reachable Temporal server, start two processes in separate terminals:

METRICS_BASE_PORT=9100 uv run python examples/example_metrics.py run all
METRICS_BASE_PORT=9102 uv run python examples/example_metrics.py run all

METRICS_BASE_PORT is an environment variable implemented by this example. It is not a Temporal-boost configuration option. A Prometheus server on the same host can scrape all four exporters:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: temporal-workers
    metrics_path: /metrics
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["127.0.0.1:9100", "127.0.0.1:9101", "127.0.0.1:9102", "127.0.0.1:9103"]

Keep Prometheus's instance label to distinguish endpoints before aggregating across replicas. Native worker metrics carry task queue labels. In the locked SDK, global_tags appear as resource metadata in target_info; they are not automatically labels on every counter. Scrape target_info alongside the metrics, and join it on job/instance when resource metadata is needed.

Ownership and failure: runtimes are built lazily in the worker's process. The worker passes its runtime to its own client. Cleanup releases worker/client/runtime references; the SDK manages native handles and provides no public Runtime.close() in the locked version. External runtime or metric meter references can extend the exporter's lifetime. Do not build a live SDK runtime in a parent and transfer it to a child: SDK runtimes do not work across forks. There is no shared-runtime API here.

An exporter initialization failure now propagates and fails worker startup, including a bind conflict. The log names the actual configured Prometheus endpoint; telemetry is never retried with metrics disabled. run all then stops peer workers, and the external supervisor propagates the failure. Configure distinct endpoints rather than relying on the first runtime that happens to bind.

Migration: older releases could continue with metrics disabled after a port conflict, leaving a partially observed service. Such deployments now fail startup. Give every runtime a unique endpoint or use an external telemetry collector. An explicit metrics=PrometheusConfig(...) takes priority over prometheus_bind_address, and follows the same failure policy.

PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR is unrelated to the SDK exporter. It is used by Python's prometheus_client multiprocess mode when that client is installed and configured separately. Temporal's SDK exporter does not write there, and Temporal-boost does not combine SDK metrics through it. The launcher's legacy automatic directory setup has been removed; any directory used by the application remains application-owned.

items.title: Interceptors
items.text: Interceptors allow you to add cross-cutting concerns like logging, metrics, or authentication.

items.title: Creating an Interceptor
items.text:
import logging
from typing import Any

from temporalio.worker import (
    ActivityInboundInterceptor,
    ExecuteActivityInput,
    ExecuteWorkflowInput,
    Interceptor,
    WorkflowInboundInterceptor,
    WorkflowInterceptorClassInput,
)


class LoggingActivityInboundInterceptor(ActivityInboundInterceptor):
    async def execute_activity(self, input: ExecuteActivityInput) -> Any:
        logging.getLogger(__name__).info("Executing activity: %s", input.fn.__name__)
        return await super().execute_activity(input)


class LoggingWorkflowInboundInterceptor(WorkflowInboundInterceptor):
    async def execute_workflow(self, input: ExecuteWorkflowInput) -> Any:
        # Use workflow.logger for replay-aware logging inside workflow code.
        from temporalio import workflow
        workflow.logger.info("Executing workflow: %s", input.type.__name__)
        return await super().execute_workflow(input)


class LoggingInterceptor(Interceptor):
    def intercept_activity(self, next: ActivityInboundInterceptor) -> ActivityInboundInterceptor:
        return LoggingActivityInboundInterceptor(next)

    def workflow_interceptor_class(
        self, input: WorkflowInterceptorClassInput
    ) -> type[WorkflowInboundInterceptor]:
        return LoggingWorkflowInboundInterceptor

items.title: Using Interceptors
items.text:
This registration fragment assumes app, my_activity, and my_workflow already exist:

worker = app.add_worker(
    "logged_worker",
    "logged_queue",
    activities=[my_activity],
    workflows=[my_workflow],
    interceptors=[LoggingInterceptor()],
)

Interceptor types use public exports from temporalio.worker. The minimum supported SDK is 1.14.1, matching the checked lockfile baseline; newer versions are allowed without an arbitrary upper bound. The base CLI uses Typer's public invocation API. Explicit BoostApp.run([...]) arguments are passed literally; run() delegates native argument handling, including Windows expansion, to Typer/Click. Embedders can pass windows_expand_args=False to disable that expansion.

items.text:
import logging
import logging.config
from contextvars import ContextVar

request_id_var: ContextVar[str | None] = ContextVar("request_id", default=None)

class ContextualFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record):
        record.request_id = request_id_var.get()
        return super().format(record)

logging_config = {
    "version": 1,
    "formatters": {
        "contextual": {
            "()": ContextualFormatter,
            "format": "%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] [%(request_id)s] %(message)s",
        },
    },
    "handlers": {
        "console": {
            "class": "logging.StreamHandler",
            "formatter": "contextual",
        },
    },
    "root": {
        "level": "INFO",
        "handlers": ["console"],
    },
}

app = BoostApp(logger_config=logging_config)

items.title: Activity Logging Decorator
items.text:
from functools import wraps
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def log_activity(func):
    @wraps(func)
    async def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        logger.info(f"Starting activity: {func.__name__}")
        try:
            result = await func(*args, **kwargs)
            logger.info(f"Completed activity: {func.__name__}")
            return result
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed activity: {func.__name__}, error: {e}")
            raise
    return wrapper

@activity.defn(name="logged_activity")
@log_activity
async def my_activity(data: str) -> str:
    return f"Processed: {data}"

items.title: Custom Worker Registration
items.text:
app.add_async_runtime("service", worker) registers an existing BaseBoostWorker subclass and assigns worker.name = "service". An internal name supplied by the class is replaced; an initial name is optional. CLI dispatch, get_registered_workers(), logs, and the worker-service thread in run all use the registered name. Keep it unchanged after registration and create a distinct instance for each app registration.

Names must be unique across Temporal, ASGI, FastStream, and custom workers. The names run, cron, exec, and all are reserved. Reusing a name or registering the same object twice in one app raises RuntimeError before changing the object or adding a command. The worker's run() signature still defines its individual CLI arguments; provide defaults for any parameters because run all calls it without arguments.

Pre-created Temporal workers retain their configuration. add_async_runtime() does not apply app endpoint/namespace/Pydantic defaults, change the existing CRON workflow ID, or register CRON commands. Configure such workers explicitly before initialization, or use add_worker() to inherit app settings and register CRON commands.

Implement run() and async shutdown() on a direct BaseBoostWorker subclass. For managed shutdown, implement thread-safe request_stop() and run cleanup on the owning loop. AsyncBoostWorker provides this lifecycle for asyncio workers, as in the following example.

The standalone examples/example_custom_worker.py requires no external service:

uv run python examples/example_custom_worker.py run all
# Ctrl+C requests managed shutdown.

It is also checked with uv run mypy examples/example_custom_worker.py.

items.title: Custom Worker Shutdown
items.text:
import asyncio

from temporal_boost import AsyncBoostWorker, BoostApp


class ServiceWorker(AsyncBoostWorker):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.name = "service"
        self.finished: asyncio.Event | None = None

    async def run_async(self) -> None:
        # Create loop-bound resources here.
        self.finished = asyncio.Event()
        await self.finished.wait()

    async def shutdown(self) -> None:
        # Close resources here, on the loop that created them.
        # This must also be safe during partial startup.
        if self.finished is not None:
            self.finished.set()


app = BoostApp("lifecycle-example", shutdown_timeout=30.0)
app.add_async_runtime("service", ServiceWorker())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

Run this example with python main.py run all. AsyncBoostWorker implements run() and the thread-safe request_stop(); keep those implementations and override run_async() and shutdown(). Cleanup runs once per invocation, including when run_async() returns normally. It must tolerate partially initialized resources and make run_async() return. A stop requested before the loop starts is remembered. Successful sequential runs create fresh loops; concurrent runs are rejected. In run all, an exception or a normal return before application shutdown stops the other workers and propagates as a failure. Finite workers must call app.stop() before returning to finish normally, or be run individually. The first failure remains primary if peer cleanup fails or times out. For AsyncBoostWorker, an error in run_async() survives its own cleanup failure too; cleanup errors during cancellation propagate instead of being mistaken for normal cancellation. Calling async shutdown() directly is reserved for code already running on the owning loop. For another threading or loop model, implement BaseBoostWorker.request_stop() using that model's thread-safe signaling API. The shutdown guide describes deadlines and current adapter limitations.

items.title: Activity Retry with Custom Logic
items.text:
from temporalio import activity
from temporalio.common import RetryPolicy
from datetime import timedelta

@activity.defn(
    name="retryable_activity",
    start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(minutes=5),
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(
        initial_interval=timedelta(seconds=1),
        backoff_coefficient=2.0,
        maximum_interval=timedelta(seconds=60),
        maximum_attempts=3,
    ),
)
async def retryable_activity(data: str) -> str:
    try:
        # Your logic here
        return process_data(data)
    except TransientError:
        # Will be retried automatically
        raise
    except PermanentError:
        # Will not be retried
        raise

items.title: Workflow Error Handling
items.text:
from temporalio import workflow
from temporalio.exceptions import ActivityError, ApplicationError

@workflow.defn(sandboxed=False, name="ErrorHandlingWorkflow")
class ErrorHandlingWorkflow:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, data: str) -> dict:
        try:
            result = await workflow.execute_activity(
                risky_activity,
                data,
                task_queue="error_queue",
                start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(minutes=5),
            )
            return {"status": "success", "result": result}
        except ActivityError as e:
            # Activity failed
            workflow.logger.error(f"Activity failed: {e}")
            return {"status": "failed", "error": str(e)}
        except ApplicationError as e:
            # Application-specific error
            workflow.logger.error(f"Application error: {e}")
            raise

items.title: Connection Pooling
items.text: SDK clients manage their connections internally. Temporal-boost workers create independent clients and runtimes; configuring a builder or creating a standalone runtime does not share it with those workers. For standalone builders, call client_builder.set_runtime(runtime) before await build(). For multiple Temporal-boost workers, follow the metrics endpoint topology.

items.title: Activity Result Caching
items.text:
For expensive activities that can be cached:

from functools import lru_cache
from temporalio import activity

# Cache at activity level (use with caution)
@activity.defn(name="cached_activity")
async def cached_activity(key: str) -> str:
    return expensive_operation(key)

# Or implement caching in workflow
@workflow.defn(sandboxed=False, name="CachedWorkflow")
class CachedWorkflow:
    def __init__(self):
        self._cache: dict[str, str] = {}

    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, key: str) -> str:
        if key in self._cache:
            return self._cache[key]

        result = await workflow.execute_activity(
            cached_activity,
            key,
            task_queue="cache_queue",
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(minutes=5),
        )
        self._cache[key] = result
        return result

items.title: Workflow Versioning
items.text:
@workflow.defn(sandboxed=False, name="VersionedWorkflow")
class VersionedWorkflow:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, data: dict) -> dict:
        version = data.get("version", 1)

        if version == 1:
            return await self._run_v1(data)
        elif version == 2:
            return await self._run_v2(data)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unsupported version: {version}")

    async def _run_v1(self, data: dict) -> dict:
        # V1 logic
        pass

    async def _run_v2(self, data: dict) -> dict:
        # V2 logic
        pass

items.title: BoostApp.__init__()
items.text:
Initialize a BoostApp instance.

BoostApp(
    name: str | None = None,
    *,
    temporal_endpoint: str | None = None,
    temporal_namespace: str | None = None,
    debug_mode: bool = False,
    use_pydantic: bool | None = None,
    logger_config: dict[str, Any] | str | Path | None = DEFAULT_LOGGING_CONFIG,
    shutdown_timeout: float = 30.0,
) -> None

Parameters:

  • name (str | None): Application name. Defaults to "temporal_generic_service".
  • temporal_endpoint (str | None): Override the imported TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST value. None inherits it.
  • temporal_namespace (str | None): Override the imported TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE value. None inherits it.

app = BoostApp(

items.title: BoostApp.add_worker()
items.text:
Add a Temporal worker to the application.

add_worker(
    worker_name: str,
    task_queue: str,
    *,
    activities: list[Callable[..., Any]] | None = None,
    workflows: list[type] | None = None,
    interceptors: list[Interceptor] | None = None,
    cron_schedule: str | None = None,
    cron_runner: MethodAsyncNoParam[Any, Any] | None = None,
    cron_workflow_id: str | None = None,
    **worker_kwargs: Any,
) -> TemporalBoostWorker

Parameters:

  • worker_name (str): Unique worker name. Cannot be reserved names: "run", "cron", "exec", "all".
  • task_queue (str): Temporal task queue name.
  • activities (list[Callable] | None): List of activity functions.
  • workflows (list[type] | None): List of workflow classes.
  • interceptors (list[Interceptor] | None): List of Temporal interceptors.
  • cron_schedule (str | None): CRON schedule string for scheduled workflows.
  • cron_runner (MethodAsyncNoParam | None): Workflow run method for CRON workers.
  • cron_workflow_id (str | None): Stable workflow ID in the configured namespace. Defaults to temporal-boost/cron/<percent-encoded task_queue>/<percent-encoded worker_name>. Empty or whitespace-only explicit IDs raise ValueError.
  • **worker_kwargs: Additional worker configuration options.

cron_schedule and cron_runner must be provided together or both omitted. Partial configuration, or an explicitly empty/whitespace-only schedule, raises ValueError during worker construction before connecting. Expression syntax is validated by the SDK/server. These rules also apply to direct TemporalBoostWorker construction. Supplying cron_workflow_id alone does not enable CRON mode. add_worker() registers commands locally; it does not create a server-side schedule.

graceful_shutdown_timeout=timedelta(...) in worker_kwargs sets the SDK activity grace period. Omission or None inherits TEMPORAL_GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT (default 30 seconds), zero is preserved, and negative durations raise ValueError at registration. This is independent of BoostApp.shutdown_timeout; see configuration.

Returns:

  • TemporalBoostWorker: The created worker instance.

Example:

worker = app.add_worker(
    "my_worker",
    "my_queue",
    activities=[my_activity],
    workflows=[MyWorkflow],
)

items.title: BoostApp.run()
items.text:
Run the application CLI.

run(args: list[str] | None = None, **kwargs: Any) -> Any

args is one list of CLI arguments. Omission or None uses sys.argv[1:]; [] stays empty and triggers the configured no-command help/usage behavior (code 2). Separate positional arguments and a single command string are unsupported: use app.run(["run", "worker_name"]).

By default Typer raises SystemExit: help and successful commands use 0; unknown commands, missing arguments, and invalid values use 2. Explicit nonzero exits are preserved. Unhandled worker errors propagate and produce a nonzero process status. In run all, a worker's SystemExit(0) or SystemExit(None) is converted to RuntimeError at the CLI boundary so coordinator failure cannot report success; a direct run_all_workers() still raises the original exception.

Options such as standalone_mode=False and prog_name="service" are forwarded to Typer. In non-standalone mode, run() returns the command's value and propagates parsing/worker exceptions (for example, click.UsageError or RuntimeError). Help returns 0. Explicit callback exits follow Typer's semantics: a SystemExit raised directly by a callback still propagates. The return value is not a general exit-status API; use the default standalone mode at a process entry point.

Example:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

For embedding, call app.run(["exec", "check"], standalone_mode=False) after registering check. Migration: callers that previously relied on run() swallowing SystemExit must now catch it explicitly or choose non-standalone mode and handle exceptions.

items.title: BoostApp.run_all_workers() and BoostApp.stop()
items.text:
run_all_workers() -> None
stop() -> None

run_all_workers() starts a thread for each registered worker and waits for a stop request or failure. In the main thread it temporarily handles SIGINT and SIGTERM. stop() requests shutdown from any thread, returns immediately, and is safe to repeat. Calls outside a run do not affect the next run. Once stopping, the coordinator calls each live worker's request_stop() and joins all threads within shutdown_timeout. It raises TimeoutError naming any remaining workers if there was no earlier failure. Otherwise the timeout is logged and the earlier exception is re-raised. Their daemon threads may continue; restarting is rejected while they remain alive. Concurrent calls are rejected too.

The first worker failure requests application shutdown and is re-raised with its original traceback after cleanup. Later failures are logged without replacing it. A normal run() return before application shutdown is a RuntimeError; finite workers must call app.stop() before returning or use an individual command. A normal return or asyncio.CancelledError / concurrent.futures.CancelledError during application shutdown is accepted. Cancellation before stop and all other exceptions (including SystemExit / KeyboardInterrupt) propagate as failures. The same ordering preserves startup and stop-request failures. The CLI converts a failure with a success SystemExit code as described above. The external multi-process supervisor propagates the first observed child failure after stopping its peers.

Workers must opt into managed stopping. Temporal, FastStream, and built-in ASGI workers support this contract; custom workers provide request_stop() or inherit AsyncBoostWorker. See Graceful Shutdown for guarantees and limitations.

items.title: BoostApp.add_async_runtime()
items.text:
add_async_runtime(worker_name: str, boost_worker: BaseBoostWorker) -> None

Register a custom worker's run() under a CLI command and include it in run all. boost_worker follows the BaseBoostWorker contract: implement synchronous run() and asynchronous shutdown(). For managed stopping, also implement the thread-safe request_stop() contract, or inherit AsyncBoostWorker as shown in the custom worker guide.

Registration assigns boost_worker.name = worker_name, replacing any previous name. This is the canonical name for run <worker_name>, get_registered_workers(), logs, and worker-<worker_name> threads in run all. The callback retains its CLI parameters; run all calls run() with no arguments. Keep the registered name unchanged and use a separate instance for each app registration.

All worker registration methods share one namespace. Reserved names (run, cron, exec, all), duplicate names across worker types, and a second registration of the same object in one app raise RuntimeError before changing its name or adding a CLI command. Registration returns None.

A pre-created TemporalBoostWorker keeps its client/runtime configuration, debug flag, and existing cron_workflow_id; this method does not apply BoostApp Temporal settings or register a cron command. This preserves its previous configuration behavior. To inherit app settings and register CRON commands, use add_worker(); otherwise configure the pre-created worker explicitly before resource initialization.

Migration: A registration alias now becomes the worker's name. Code that needs the old name for application-specific data should store it separately. Multiple aliases for one worker instance are rejected; create distinct worker instances. The unused private CRON/ASGI registration lists have been removed; use get_registered_workers() to inspect registered workers.

items.title: CLI Process Runner
items.text:
Application strings use module:attribute.nested with dotted identifiers. The importer first uses Python's normal import path, then tries the current directory and its immediate parent only for a missing target module/package. Missing dependencies and application exceptions propagate unchanged. Malformed strings, unavailable targets, and missing attributes produce distinct ValueError messages; target/attribute lookup errors retain their original exception as the cause.

Failed calls restore sys.path; successful fallback imports retain only the directory that resolved the target for subsequent application imports. There is no recursive directory search or module-cache reset. See application import lookup.

The external launcher supports --workers N --shutdown-timeout SECONDS before the application path. The shutdown timeout applies when --workers > 1, defaults to 30 seconds, and must be finite and non-negative.

from temporal_boost.cli.process_runner import run_multiprocess

run_multiprocess(
    app_path: str,
    number_of_processes: int,
    arguments: list[str],
    *,
    shutdown_timeout: float = 30.0,
) -> None

Starts the same application command in each child. It observes every child independently, stops peers on the first nonzero child exit, joins terminated children, and closes process handles. No automatic restart occurs. Ordinary completion returns None once all children succeed. Failure raises SystemExit with the first observed positive child status; signal termination -N maps to 128 + N. Startup/cleanup exceptions propagate without replacing an earlier failure. A failure carrying SystemExit(0) or SystemExit(None) becomes RuntimeError. Invalid process counts or timeout values raise ValueError before processes are created.

For BoostApp, a command selecting ASGI with number_of_processes > 1 raises a usage error in the child before workers start; the parent propagates exit code 2. This includes run all with any BaseAsgiWorker and run <asgi-name>, across all backends. Selecting a Temporal worker, CRON, exec, or help remains allowed even if the application registers ASGI. The check uses the actual command callback after parsing, and never imports the application in the parent. There is no shared-socket mode. See ASGI and External Processes.

The parent first requests managed stopping through dedicated one-way pipes and child watchers, then closes the stop endpoints. One grace deadline covers all children, followed by terminate (up to 5 seconds) and kill (up to 5 seconds). Main-thread invocation temporarily handles SIGINT/SIGTERM and restores the previous handlers; after cleanup the parent exits with 130/143 unless a failure determined the result. Repeated signals keep the first request and its deadlines. This timeout is independent of the application and SDK budgets. See Multi-process Supervision for command examples, managed worker requirements, and migration.

items.title: Worker Stop Contract
items.text:
BaseBoostWorker.request_stop() -> bool is a non-blocking, thread-safe stop request. Implementations must tolerate repeats and requests during startup. Return True when supported; the default returns False. Async cleanup belongs on the resource-owning loop.

AsyncBoostWorker (exported from temporal_boost and temporal_boost.workers) provides this contract for asyncio workers. Call super().__init__(), set name, implement async run_async() and shutdown(), and inherit run() and request_stop(). The helper owns the loop, runs shutdown() once per run, and waits for run_async() to return. shutdown() must handle partial startup and unblock run_async(). If run_async() fails, its exception survives a subsequent cleanup failure, which is logged. When run_async() is cancelled and cleanup fails, the cleanup error propagates so normal cancellation cannot hide failed cleanup. See the example.

items.text:
Temporal worker class.

Endpoint and namespace precedence is the last explicit worker configuration → BoostApp parameters → environment values captured at import → built-in defaults (localhost:7233, default). Each field is selected independently. See configuration priority.

items.title: TemporalBoostWorker.configure_temporal_client()
items.text:
Configure the Temporal client before initialization or after the previous run has finished cleanup. Raises RuntimeError once initialization starts, or while a lifecycle is building, running, or stopping. The call never reconnects a live client or changes its SDK worker. Rejected calls leave builders unchanged.

configure_temporal_client(
    *,
    target_host: str | None = None,
    namespace: str | None = None,
    api_key: str | None = None,
    identity: str | None = None,
    tls: bool | None = None,
    use_pydantic_data_converter: bool | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> None

Parameters:

  • target_host (str | None): Temporal server address.
  • namespace (str | None): Temporal namespace.
  • api_key (str | None): API key for Temporal Cloud.
  • identity (str | None): Client identity.
  • tls (bool | None): Enable TLS.
  • use_pydantic_data_converter (bool | None): True enables Pydantic; False disables automatic Pydantic selection. None inherits the environment on initial configuration and leaves an existing builder unchanged. An explicit data_converter in kwargs takes priority.
  • **kwargs: Additional client options.

On an existing builder, omitted fields and None keep their previous values. Explicit empty strings are passed to setters unchanged; they do not reset to environment defaults. Explicit tls=False overrides an imported True value. Configure before initialization; these options do not reconnect an active client.

Example:

worker.configure_temporal_client(
    target_host="temporal.example.com:7233",
    namespace="production",
    use_pydantic_data_converter=True,

items.title: TemporalBoostWorker.configure_temporal_runtime()
items.text:
Configure an independent, worker-owned Temporal runtime before first use. Concurrent workers need distinct Prometheus endpoints; runtimes are not shared automatically. Each process must expose every worker's endpoint for scraping. See Metrics Across Workers and Processes.

Raises RuntimeError after a runtime has been created or during an active lifecycle. Reading temporal_client_runtime creates the runtime and fixes these settings, including before run(). After run cleanup releases resources, this method configures the next run. It never replaces a live runtime. See configuration lifetime.

configure_temporal_runtime(
    *,
    logging: LoggingConfig | None = None,
    metrics: OpenTelemetryConfig | PrometheusConfig | MetricBuffer | None = None,
    global_tags: Mapping[str, str] | None = None,
    attach_service_name: bool = True,
    metric_prefix: str | None = None,
    prometheus_bind_address: str | None = config.PROMETHEUS_BIND_ADDRESS,
    prometheus_counters_total_suffix: bool | None = config.PROMETHEUS_COUNTERS_TOTAL_SUFFIX,
    prometheus_unit_suffix: bool | None = config.PROMETHEUS_UNIT_SUFFIX,
    prometheus_durations_as_seconds: bool | None = config.PROMETHEUS_DURATIONS_AS_SECONDS,
) -> None

Parameters:

  • logging (LoggingConfig | None): Custom logging configuration.
  • metrics (OpenTelemetryConfig | PrometheusConfig | MetricBuffer | None): Metrics configuration.
  • global_tags (Mapping[str, str] | None): Global tags for metrics.
  • attach_service_name (bool): Attach service name to metrics.
  • metric_prefix (str | None): Prefix for metric names.
  • prometheus_bind_address (str | None): Prometheus metrics bind address.
  • prometheus_counters_total_suffix (bool | None): Append _total to counters.
  • prometheus_unit_suffix (bool | None): Append unit suffix to metrics.
  • prometheus_durations_as_seconds (bool | None): Express durations in seconds.

Example:

worker.configure_temporal_runtime(
    prometheus_bind_address="0.0.0.0:9090",
    global_tags={"environment": "production"},

items.title: TemporalBoostWorker.run()
items.text:
Consume the worker's task queue. This never registers a CRON workflow, including when CRON parameters are configured. run <name> uses this method; run all uses it for every registered worker.

run() -> None

Example:

worker.run()

items.title: TemporalBoostWorker.cron()
items.text:
Run the worker as a CRON worker.

Available as cron <name> only when both CRON parameters are configured. Calling this method directly without them raises RuntimeError before creating a loop or connecting. It registers once per process start, then keeps consuming the task queue until stopped.

Atomically starts or reuses the ID using WorkflowIDConflictPolicy.USE_EXISTING. Closed IDs are rejected with WorkflowAlreadyStartedError using WorkflowIDReusePolicy.REJECT_DUPLICATE, subject to server history retention. Reuse preserves the existing schedule and configuration. Local shutdown does not cancel the server-side workflow. See CRON identity and the UUID migration procedure.

cron() -> None

Example:

worker.cron()

Both commands own their event loop and use one lifecycle for startup, execution, and cleanup. A stop during startup cancels pending connection work. CRON cleanup completes the local wait and cancels any pending registration call, then stops the SDK worker. The adapter owns the SDK run() task and uses its public shutdown() API; it does not also enter the SDK async context manager. Normal run() does not register a CRON workflow. Local stop does not delete a server-side workflow.

Sequential runs are supported and rebuild the client, runtime, and SDK worker on the next loop. Concurrent run() / cron() calls on the same adapter raise RuntimeError. Startup and execution errors propagate after cleanup; later cleanup errors are logged without replacing the original error. Unexpected cancellation now propagates too. SDK validation failure before starting does not wait on an SDK shutdown() that could never finish. No public Client/Runtime close API exists in the supported SDK: the adapter releases its and its builders' references, and does not close caller-supplied executors or invent close methods. External references may keep SDK objects alive.

items.title: TemporalBoostWorker.request_stop() and TemporalBoostWorker.shutdown()
items.text:
def request_stop() -> bool
async def shutdown() -> None

request_stop() returns True and requests stop without waiting, from any thread. Repeats are safe; a request before the first run is remembered and prevents resource creation. Requests after stopping have no effect on the next run. shutdown() before/after a run is a no-op. During a run it must be called on the owning loop, requests stop, and waits for lifecycle completion, including any error. Concurrent waiters share cleanup; cancelling a waiter does not cancel the lifecycle. A foreign-loop call raises RuntimeError directing callers to request_stop(). Use request_stop() inside worker callbacks too.

SDK shutdown is invoked at most once for an active SDK run. After SDK run() has already completed, its result is retrieved without another SDK shutdown call. On a shutdown failure the adapter cancels and joins its SDK task before releasing references. A stuck SDK operation can still exceed its activity grace period; BoostApp.shutdown_timeout bounds the coordinator's wait, not the SDK operation itself.

items.title: Lifecycle states
items.text:
The read-only state property reports:

Value Meaning created Constructed; no active lifecycle building Creating runtime, connecting client, and constructing the SDK worker running SDK run task started; CRON registration may still be pending stopping Cancelling startup/CRON work and waiting for SDK cleanup stopped Adapter and builder resource references released; another run is allowed

Early stop or failure may skip running. Configure options before initialization and before a run. created does not imply the runtime is absent: the lazy runtime property can initialize it without starting a lifecycle. After stopped, configuration is available again until the next initialization.

  • temporal_cron_runner (MethodAsyncNoParam): Get CRON runner method.
  • cron_workflow_id (str): Read-only resolved CRON workflow ID.
  • state: Current lifecycle state. Client and SDK worker properties raise after cleanup until rebuilt.

items.title: Configuration Constants
items.text:
Environment defaults are available as constants in temporal_boost.temporal.config. They are read once during the first package import; .env files are not loaded automatically. Prepare the environment before importing the package or starting the CLI. Later os.environ changes do not update these constants or configure existing SDK objects. See environment loading.

  • CLIENT_NAMESPACE: Temporal namespace
  • CLIENT_TLS: TLS enabled flag
  • CLIENT_API_KEY: API key
  • CLIENT_IDENTITY: Client identity
  • USE_PYDANTIC_DATA_CONVERTER: Pydantic converter flag
  • MAX_CONCURRENT_WORKFLOW_TASKS: Max concurrent workflow tasks
  • MAX_CONCURRENT_ACTIVITIES: Max concurrent activities
  • MAX_CONCURRENT_LOCAL_ACTIVITIES: Max concurrent local activities
  • MAX_WORKFLOW_TASK_POLLS: Max workflow task polls
  • MAX_ACTIVITY_TASK_POLLS: Max activity task polls
  • NONSTICKY_STICKY_RATIO: Non-sticky to sticky ratio
  • GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT: SDK activity grace period (timedelta, default 30 seconds), independent of application shutdown budget
  • PROMETHEUS_BIND_ADDRESS: Prometheus bind address
  • PROMETHEUS_COUNTERS_TOTAL_SUFFIX: Counters total suffix flag
  • PROMETHEUS_UNIT_SUFFIX: Unit suffix flag
  • PROMETHEUS_DURATIONS_AS_SECONDS: Durations as seconds flag

For detailed configuration options, see Configuration Guide.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: Temporal-boost uses environment variables for defaults and provides explicit application and worker configuration. This guide covers the available options, their precedence, and when they are read.

items.title: Table of Contents

items.title: Environment Loading
items.text:
temporal_boost.temporal.config reads environment variables once, when the package is first imported. Set the environment before importing temporal_boost or any module that imports it. Changing os.environ afterward does not update these constants, even for a newly constructed app or builder. To select different settings after import, pass explicit arguments or configure the worker before initialization; see when configuration becomes fixed.

The package does not load .env files automatically. Load one before importing the package, or prepare the process environment externally. See the startup example. The installed temporal-boost command imports the package before importing your app module, so a .env loader inside that module is too late for the CLI's configuration defaults. Prepare its environment before starting the command.

items.title: Temporal Client Configuration
items.text: These settings control how workers connect to the Temporal server.

items.title: TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST
items.text:
Type: String Default: localhost:7233 Description: Temporal server address (host:port)

export TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST=temporal.example.com:7233

items.title: TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE
items.text:
Type: String Default: default Description: Temporal namespace to use

export TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE=production

items.title: TEMPORAL_TLS
items.text:
Type: Boolean Default: false Description: Enable TLS for Temporal connections

export TEMPORAL_TLS=true

Accepts: true, 1, yes (case-insensitive)

items.title: TEMPORAL_API_KEY
items.text:
Type: String Default: None Description: API key for Temporal Cloud or secured clusters

export TEMPORAL_API_KEY=your-api-key-here

Security Note: Never commit API keys to version control. Use secrets management.

items.title: TEMPORAL_IDENTITY
items.text:
Type: String Default: None Description: Client identity for Temporal connections

export TEMPORAL_IDENTITY=worker-1

items.title: TEMPORAL_USE_PYDANTIC_DATA_CONVERTER
items.text:
Type: Boolean Default: false Description: Use Pydantic data converter for serialization

export TEMPORAL_USE_PYDANTIC_DATA_CONVERTER=true

When enabled, Temporal-boost uses Pydantic models for data serialization, providing better type safety and validation.

BoostApp(use_pydantic=...) and use_pydantic_data_converter on TemporalClientBuilder or worker.configure_temporal_client() use the same selection rule when creating a client builder:

Argument Behavior None (default) Inherit TEMPORAL_USE_PYDANTIC_DATA_CONVERTER True Enable the SDK Pydantic converter False Disable automatic Pydantic selection, even when the environment enables it

An explicit data_converter passed to TemporalClientBuilder, set_kwargs(), or worker.configure_temporal_client() takes priority over both the flag and environment setting. Disabling the flag preserves that converter. Without an explicit converter, disabling the flag leaves the Temporal SDK's default converter in use.

app = BoostApp(use_pydantic=False)  # Overrides an environment value of true
worker = app.add_worker("example", "example-queue", activities=[my_activity])
worker.configure_temporal_client(data_converter=custom_converter)  # Explicit converter takes priority

Before client initialization, or after run cleanup, configure_temporal_client() updates the flag only when given True or False; None leaves the previous selection unchanged. Late calls raise RuntimeError; see when configuration becomes fixed. Use builder.set_pydantic_data_converter(enabled=False) to disable Pydantic on a standalone builder; builder.set_pydantic_data_converter() still enables it. Each subsequent build() uses the current selection without retaining a converter automatically added by an earlier build. These changes apply to future client builds; they do not reconfigure an already connected client.

Migration: Code that relied on False enabling Pydantic must pass True. Code that supplied both an explicit converter and an enabled Pydantic flag now uses the explicit converter; remove it to use the SDK Pydantic converter.

items.title: Worker Configuration
items.text:
These settings control worker behavior and resource limits.

The six concurrency, poll-count, and polling-ratio options below use the environment/default only when the corresponding worker argument is omitted or None. Selected values are validated when TemporalWorkerBuilder is constructed, including through BoostApp.add_worker():

Worker argument Accepted values max_concurrent_workflow_tasks Positive integer max_concurrent_activities Positive integer max_concurrent_local_activities Positive integer max_concurrent_workflow_task_polls Positive integer max_concurrent_activity_task_polls Positive integer nonsticky_to_sticky_poll_ratio Finite, non-negative int or float, including 0.0; no upper cap

Wrong types, including booleans and numeric strings, raise TypeError; out-of-range values raise ValueError. Counts reject floats, including 1.0. Explicit values do not silently fall back: replace an old zero count with None or omit it to select configuration. A selected zero or negative count from the environment also raises ValueError. A valid explicit argument can override an invalid configured default. Environment parsing still occurs at import time; malformed integer/float text retains the existing parser fallback to the framework default.

The SDK enforces additional constraints during build(), including workflow task concurrency and workflow poll counts of at least two when workflow caching is enabled (max_cached_workflows > 0). With caching disabled, one is valid. The builder's non-negative, finite ratio check rejects unusable settings that SDK Core itself does not range-check; it does not impose a 1.0 upper limit.

app.add_worker("worker", "queue", workflows=[MyWorkflow], nonsticky_to_sticky_poll_ratio=0.0)

The zero ratio reaches the SDK unchanged. The SDK still uses at least one poller per sticky/non-sticky queue when caching is enabled; zero does not disable non-sticky polling.

items.title: TEMPORAL_MAX_CONCURRENT_WORKFLOW_TASKS
items.text:
Type: Integer Default: 300 Description: Maximum concurrent workflow tasks per worker

export TEMPORAL_MAX_CONCURRENT_WORKFLOW_TASKS=500

Increase for high workflow throughput, decrease to limit resource usage.

items.title: TEMPORAL_MAX_CONCURRENT_ACTIVITIES
items.text:
Type: Integer Default: 300 Description: Maximum concurrent activity executions per worker

export TEMPORAL_MAX_CONCURRENT_ACTIVITIES=200

Tune based on your activity workload and available resources.

items.title: TEMPORAL_MAX_CONCURRENT_LOCAL_ACTIVITIES
items.text:
Type: Integer Default: 100 Description: Maximum concurrent local activity executions

export TEMPORAL_MAX_CONCURRENT_LOCAL_ACTIVITIES=50

Local activities execute in the same process as workflows.

items.title: TEMPORAL_MAX_WORKFLOW_TASK_POLLS
items.text:
Type: Integer Default: 10 Description: Maximum concurrent workflow task polls

export TEMPORAL_MAX_WORKFLOW_TASK_POLLS=20

Controls how many workflow tasks can be polled simultaneously.

items.title: TEMPORAL_MAX_ACTIVITY_TASK_POLLS
items.text:
Type: Integer Default: 10 Description: Maximum concurrent activity task polls

export TEMPORAL_MAX_ACTIVITY_TASK_POLLS=20

Controls how many activity tasks can be polled simultaneously.

items.title: TEMPORAL_NONSTICKY_TO_STICKY_RATIO
items.text:
Type: Float Default: 0.2 Description: Ratio of non-sticky to sticky workflow task polls

export TEMPORAL_NONSTICKY_TO_STICKY_RATIO=0.3

Sticky workflows improve performance by keeping workflow state in memory.

items.title: TEMPORAL_GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT
items.text:
Type: Integer (seconds) Default: 30 Description: Activity grace period passed to the Temporal SDK worker as graceful_shutdown_timeout

export TEMPORAL_GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT=60

When SDK worker shutdown begins, activities get this grace period to finish before the SDK requests cancellation. Zero requests cancellation without a grace period. SDK shutdown still waits for activities to finish; an activity that ignores cancellation can keep shutdown waiting beyond this duration.

Override the environment per worker with a datetime.timedelta:

from datetime import timedelta

worker = app.add_worker(
    "payments",
    "payments_queue",
    activities=[process_payment],
    graceful_shutdown_timeout=timedelta(seconds=45),
)

An explicit value, including timedelta(0), takes priority. Omission or None uses the environment constant, read when configuration is imported; the fallback is 30 seconds. Invalid integer text uses the same fallback. A selected negative duration raises ValueError when the worker builder is created. An explicit non-negative value can override a negative environment value.

Behavior change: workers omitting this option now receive the framework's environment/default grace period (30 seconds by default). Previously this setting was ignored and the SDK defaulted to zero unless a value was passed explicitly through worker kwargs.

The application coordinator has a separate budget, BoostApp(shutdown_timeout=30.0), for joining all worker threads. The external launcher's --shutdown-timeout (default 30 seconds) sets a separate shared child-process grace period, followed by up to 5 seconds after terminate and 5 seconds after kill. Give the outer process budget enough time for the inner coordinator and SDK cleanup. This setting changes neither budget and does not initiate shutdown. The Temporal adapter participates in managed stopping through request_stop(); its SDK cleanup still depends on activities respecting cancellation. See Graceful Shutdown for current guarantees and limitations.

items.title: Prometheus Metrics Configuration
items.text: These settings control Prometheus metrics collection and export.

items.title: TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_BIND_ADDRESS
items.text:
Type: String Default: None Description: Bind address for Prometheus metrics endpoint

export TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0:9090

When set, each Temporal worker runtime exposes /metrics at this address. Concurrent runtimes need distinct endpoints; a bind conflict fails startup instead of disabling telemetry. Override the address per worker with configure_temporal_runtime(), and allocate separate ports or network addresses for each process. --workers N does not assign metrics ports. Scrape every endpoint; see Metrics Across Workers and Processes.

The SDK exporter does not use PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR; that directory does not aggregate SDK metrics.

items.title: TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_COUNTERS_TOTAL_SUFFIX
items.text:
Type: Boolean Default: false Description: Append _total suffix to counter metrics

export TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_COUNTERS_TOTAL_SUFFIX=true

items.title: TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_UNIT_SUFFIX
items.text:
Type: Boolean Default: false Description: Append unit suffix to metric names

export TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_UNIT_SUFFIX=true

items.title: TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_DURATIONS_AS_SECONDS
items.text:
Type: Boolean Default: false Description: Express durations in seconds instead of milliseconds

export TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_DURATIONS_AS_SECONDS=true

items.title: Runtime Configuration
items.text:
Runtime configuration is done programmatically. See Advanced Usage for details.

The defaults for prometheus_bind_address, prometheus_counters_total_suffix, prometheus_unit_suffix, and prometheus_durations_as_seconds are captured when TemporalRuntimeBuilder.__init__() and worker.configure_temporal_runtime() are defined during import. Changing os.environ or even assigning new values to config.PROMETHEUS_* afterward does not change omitted arguments. Supply explicit runtime arguments to change them before runtime creation.

Each configure_temporal_runtime() call replaces the runtime configuration; omitted fields return to their function defaults. An explicit metrics backend takes priority over the bind address. With metrics=None, passing prometheus_bind_address=None disables the implicit Prometheus exporter, even if the imported environment supplied an address. Explicit False or None for a Prometheus suffix/duration flag produces False; None does not re-read the environment.

items.title: When Configuration Becomes Fixed
items.text:
Configure a Temporal worker before starting it. Settings become fixed at these points:

Worker condition Runtime configuration Client configuration Created, no resources initialized Allowed Allowed Runtime created through temporal_client_runtime, client not initialized Raises RuntimeError Allowed Client/SDK worker initialization started or completed Raises RuntimeError Raises RuntimeError Lifecycle is building, running, or stopping Raises RuntimeError Raises RuntimeError Run cleanup completed (stopped), resources released Allowed for the next run Allowed for the next run

The temporal_client_runtime property creates and caches a runtime when first read, even before a run. This can bind a Prometheus port. Set runtime options before reading it. Repeated reads return the same object; reconfiguration is rejected without changing its builder. The created lifecycle state means no run is active, so it can still contain a runtime initialized through this property.

Rejected client calls also leave both builders and SDK objects unchanged. There is no automatic reconnect, runtime replacement, or live update of an SDK worker. After a run or startup failure has completed cleanup, both configuration methods are available again. The next run builds fresh objects using those settings. Reading temporal_client_runtime after cleanup creates a new runtime and fixes its options again. A failed runtime constructor that leaves no cached runtime can be reconfigured before retrying, provided no lifecycle is active.

worker = app.add_worker("consumer", "queue", activities=[my_activity])
worker.configure_temporal_runtime(prometheus_bind_address="127.0.0.1:9101")
worker.configure_temporal_client(namespace="production")
# Optional inspection now creates the runtime and fixes its telemetry options:
runtime = worker.temporal_client_runtime

Migration: Move configuration calls before run()/cron() and before the first runtime property read. For a later change, request stop, wait for the run to return and cleanup to complete, then configure the next run. To discard an initialized preview runtime without running the adapter, create a new worker instead of replacing its runtime. External references may keep the old runtime/exporter alive, so release them before reusing its port.

SDK worker options such as activities, interceptors, and concurrency are supplied when constructing the adapter or calling app.add_worker(); use a new adapter to change those options. Standalone TemporalClientBuilder/TemporalWorkerBuilder instances remain mutable: their setters affect future builds and do not alter objects already returned by build().

items.title: Configuration Priority
items.text:
Endpoint and namespace are selected independently in this order (highest to lowest priority):

  1. Explicit worker configuration: the last non-None target_host or namespace supplied to configure_temporal_client() before client initialization.
  2. BoostApp initialization parameters: temporal_endpoint and temporal_namespace.
  3. Imported environment values: TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST and TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE.
  4. Built-in defaults: localhost:7233 and default.

When an existing worker's client builder is configured again, omitted fields and None leave its previous values unchanged. Setting only the namespace preserves the selected endpoint. A standalone TemporalClientBuilder has no app layer: constructor arguments override the imported configuration, and subsequent setters override its stored values for future builds.

export TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST=temporal.prod:7233
export TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE=production

from temporal_boost import BoostApp

# The app endpoint wins over the environment; namespace still comes from the environment.
app = BoostApp(temporal_endpoint="temporal.dev:7233")
worker = app.add_worker("consumer", "queue", activities=[my_activity])
# This worker connects to temporal.dev:7233 in the isolated namespace.
worker.configure_temporal_client(namespace="isolated")
worker.configure_temporal_client(target_host=None)  # Keeps temporal.dev:7233

Other fields have their own selection rules:

Fields Selection rule Client string constructor arguments (target_host, namespace, api_key, identity) None or an empty string falls back to imported config. Worker configuration and app endpoint/namespace updates use setters, which preserve an explicit empty string. Empty strings do not reset configuration and may be rejected by the SDK. tls None on initial client configuration inherits imported config; explicit False overrides True. On an existing worker builder, None leaves the setting unchanged. Pydantic flag / data_converter Explicit converter wins over the flag; the flag distinguishes None, False, and True. See converter selection. Worker counts, ratio, and activity grace period Only None selects imported config. Zero is valid for ratio and grace period; counts must be positive. See worker configuration. Prometheus defaults Omitted arguments use defaults captured during import; explicit arguments follow the runtime rules.

items.title: Using Configuration Files
items.text:
For direct script execution, install python-dotenv separately and load the file before any import of the package or your worker modules:

from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv(".env")  # Must run before importing temporal_boost

from temporal_boost import BoostApp

app = BoostApp()

By default, load_dotenv() preserves variables already present in the process environment. This controls how the environment is prepared; the explicit app/worker precedence above still applies.

items.title: Configuration Validation
items.text:
Validate configuration at startup:

import os
from temporal_boost import BoostApp

def validate_config():
    """Validate required configuration."""
    required_vars = [
        "TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST",
        "TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE",
    ]

    missing = [var for var in required_vars if not os.getenv(var)]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"Missing required environment variables: {missing}")

validate_config()
app = BoostApp()

items.title: Startup Environment and Explicit Overrides
items.text:
Prepare environment defaults before the first package import in a fresh process:

import os

# Set defaults before importing temporal_boost or your application modules.
os.environ["TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST"] = "localhost:7233"
os.environ["TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE"] = "test"

from temporal_boost import BoostApp

app = BoostApp()

If the package has already been imported, use explicit settings for a new app or a worker whose client has not been initialized:

from temporal_boost import BoostApp

app = BoostApp(temporal_endpoint="localhost:7233", temporal_namespace="test")
worker = app.add_worker("consumer", "queue", activities=[my_activity])
worker.configure_temporal_client(namespace="another-test")

These calls configure future resource creation. They do not update an active client or runtime.

items.title: Configuration Tips
items.text:
1. Use environment-specific files: .env.development, .env.production
  2. Never commit secrets: Use secrets management for API keys
  3. Document defaults: Make configuration defaults clear in documentation
  4. Validate early: Check configuration at application startup
  5. Use types: Convert string environment variables to appropriate types
  6. Monitor configuration: Log configuration values (without secrets) at startup

items.title: Pattern 1: Environment-Based
items.text:
Run this bootstrap before importing temporal_boost or your application modules:

import os

env = os.getenv("ENVIRONMENT", "development")
if env == "production":
    os.environ.setdefault("TEMPORAL_TLS", "true")
    os.environ.setdefault("TEMPORAL_PROMETHEUS_BIND_ADDRESS", "0.0.0.0:9090")

from temporal_boost import BoostApp

app = BoostApp()

items.title: Pattern 2: Configuration Class
items.text:
An application-owned settings class reads the environment independently. Pass its values explicitly to BoostApp or worker configuration; creating the settings object does not update package constants.

from dataclasses import dataclass
import os

@dataclass
class TemporalConfig:
    host: str
    namespace: str
    tls: bool
    api_key: str | None = None

    @classmethod
    def from_env(cls):
        return cls(
            host=os.getenv("TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST", "localhost:7233"),
            namespace=os.getenv("TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE", "default"),
            tls=os.getenv("TEMPORAL_TLS", "false").lower() == "true",
            api_key=os.getenv("TEMPORAL_API_KEY"),
        )

config = TemporalConfig.from_env()

items.title: Pattern 3: Pydantic Settings
items.text:
from pydantic import BaseSettings

class TemporalSettings(BaseSettings):
    temporal_target_host: str = "localhost:7233"
    temporal_namespace: str = "default"
    temporal_tls: bool = False
    temporal_api_key: str | None = None

    class Config:
        env_prefix = "TEMPORAL_"
        case_sensitive = False

settings = TemporalSettings()

items.title: Security Best Practices
items.text:
1. Never log secrets: Filter out API keys from logs
  2. Use secrets management: AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, etc.
  3. Rotate credentials: Regularly rotate API keys
  4. Use TLS in production: Always enable TLS for production
  5. Restrict access: Use network policies to restrict Temporal access
  6. Audit configuration: Log configuration changes in production

items.title: Check Current Configuration
items.text:
import os
from temporal_boost.temporal import config

print(f"Host: {config.TARGET_HOST}")
print(f"Namespace: {config.CLIENT_NAMESPACE}")
print(f"TLS: {config.CLIENT_TLS}")

items.title: Validate Configuration
items.text:
from temporal_boost.temporal import config

def validate():
    assert config.TARGET_HOST, "TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST not set"
    assert config.CLIENT_NAMESPACE, "TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE not set"
    if config.CLIENT_TLS and not config.CLIENT_API_KEY:
        print("Warning: TLS enabled but no API key provided")

validate()

items.title: Creating application
items.text: This guide covers everything you need to know about creating Temporal-boost applications, from basic setup to advanced patterns.

items.title: Table of Contents
items.text:

  • Defining Workflows
  • Adding Workers
  • CRON Workers
  • ASGI Workers

items.title: Application Structure
items.text:
A typical Temporal-boost application follows this structure:

my_app/
├── main.py              # Application entry point
├── activities.py        # Activity definitions
├── workflows.py         # Workflow definitions
├── config.py            # Configuration (optional)
└── requirements.txt     # Dependencies

items.title: BoostApp Initialization
items.text:
The BoostApp class is the central component of your application. Initialize it at the start of your application:

from temporal_boost import BoostApp

app = BoostApp(
    name="my-service",              # Application name (optional)
    temporal_endpoint=None,          # Override TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST (optional)
    temporal_namespace=None,         # Override TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE (optional)
    debug_mode=False,                # Enable debug mode (optional)
    use_pydantic=None,               # Override Pydantic converter (optional)
    logger_config=None,              # Custom logging config (optional)
)

items.title: Configuration Priority
items.text:
Endpoint and namespace are selected independently in this order (highest to lowest priority):

  1. Explicit worker configuration via worker.configure_temporal_client(target_host=..., namespace=...)
  2. BoostApp initialization parameters
  3. Environment variables read at import
  4. Built-in default values (localhost:7233 and default)

For example, with TEMPORAL_TARGET_HOST=temporal.prod:7233 in the environment, BoostApp(temporal_endpoint="temporal.dev:7233") selects temporal.dev:7233. A later explicit worker configuration can override that address before client initialization. On an existing builder, omitted fields and None leave previous settings unchanged; the last explicit value for each field wins.

Environment values are read when temporal_boost is first imported. The package does not load .env automatically, and changing os.environ after import does not update configuration defaults. Load environment files before the first package import, or prepare the environment before starting the installed CLI. Boolean flags, numeric options, empty strings, and runtime defaults have distinct rules; see the configuration guide and environment loading.

items.title: Defining Activities
items.text: Activities are functions that perform actual work. They should be deterministic-free and can perform I/O operations.

items.title: Basic Activity
items.text:
from temporalio import activity

@activity.defn(name="process_payment")
async def process_payment(amount: float, currency: str) -> dict:
    """Process a payment transaction."""
    # Your business logic here
    return {"status": "success", "amount": amount, "currency": currency}

items.title: Activity with Pydantic Models
items.text:
Using Pydantic models provides type safety and validation:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from temporalio import activity

class PaymentRequest(BaseModel):
    amount: float
    currency: str
    customer_id: str

class PaymentResponse(BaseModel):
    transaction_id: str
    status: str
    amount: float

@activity.defn(name="process_payment")
async def process_payment(request: PaymentRequest) -> PaymentResponse:
    """Process a payment with type-safe models."""
    # Process payment...
    return PaymentResponse(
        transaction_id="tx_123",
        status="completed",
        amount=request.amount,
    )

items.title: Activity with Retry Options
items.text:
Activities can have custom retry policies:

from temporalio import activity
from temporalio.common import RetryPolicy

@activity.defn(
    name="unreliable_api_call",
    start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(seconds=30),
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(
        initial_interval=timedelta(seconds=1),
        backoff_coefficient=2.0,
        maximum_interval=timedelta(seconds=60),
        maximum_attempts=5,
    ),
)
async def unreliable_api_call(url: str) -> dict:
    """Activity with custom retry policy."""
    import httpx
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        response = await client.get(url)
        return response.json()

items.title: Activity Best Practices
items.text:
• ✅ Keep activities idempotent when possible
  • ✅ Use appropriate timeouts (start_to_close_timeout)
  • ✅ Handle errors gracefully
  • ✅ Use Pydantic models for complex data structures
  • ✅ Log important operations
  • ❌ Don't use random numbers or current time in activities
  • ❌ Don't perform operations that can't be retried

items.title: Defining Workflows
items.text: Workflows orchestrate activities and define business logic. They must be deterministic.

items.title: Basic Workflow
items.text:
from datetime import timedelta
from temporalio import workflow

@workflow.defn(sandboxed=False, name="OrderProcessingWorkflow")
class OrderProcessingWorkflow:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, order_id: str) -> dict:
        """Process an order through multiple steps."""
        # Step 1: Validate order
        validation_result = await workflow.execute_activity(
            validate_order,
            order_id,
            task_queue="order_queue",
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(minutes=5),
        )

        if not validation_result["valid"]:
            return {"status": "failed", "reason": "validation_failed"}

        # Step 2: Process payment
        payment_result = await workflow.execute_activity(
            process_payment,
            validation_result["amount"],
            task_queue="payment_queue",
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(minutes=10),
        )

        # Step 3: Fulfill order
        fulfillment_result = await workflow.execute_activity(
            fulfill_order,
            order_id,
            task_queue="fulfillment_queue",
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(minutes=30),
        )

        return {
            "status": "completed",
            "order_id": order_id,
            "payment": payment_result,
            "fulfillment": fulfillment_result,
        }

items.title: Workflow with Signals
items.text:
Signals allow external systems to send data to running workflows:

from temporalio import workflow

@workflow.defn(sandboxed=False, name="ApprovalWorkflow")
class ApprovalWorkflow:
    def __init__(self):
        self.approved = False
        self.rejected = False

    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, request_id: str) -> dict:
        """Wait for approval signal."""
        await workflow.wait_condition(lambda: self.approved or self.rejected)

        if self.approved:
            return {"status": "approved", "request_id": request_id}
        return {"status": "rejected", "request_id": request_id}

    @workflow.signal(name="approve")
    def approve(self) -> None:
        """Signal handler for approval."""
        self.approved = True

    @workflow.signal(name="reject")
    def reject(self) -> None:
        """Signal handler for rejection."""
        self.rejected = True

items.title: Workflow with Queries
items.text:
Queries allow reading workflow state without affecting execution:

from temporalio import workflow

@workflow.defn(sandboxed=False, name="OrderStatusWorkflow")
class OrderStatusWorkflow:
    def __init__(self):
        self.status = "pending"
        self.progress = 0

    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, order_id: str) -> dict:
        """Process order and update status."""
        self.status = "processing"
        await workflow.execute_activity(
            process_order,
            order_id,
            task_queue="order_queue",
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(minutes=30),
        )
        self.status = "completed"
        self.progress = 100
        return {"status": self.status, "order_id": order_id}

    @workflow.query(name="status")
    def get_status(self) -> dict:
        """Query workflow status."""
        return {"status": self.status, "progress": self.progress}

items.text:
• ✅ Keep workflows deterministic (no random, no time, no I/O)
  • ✅ Use appropriate timeouts for activities
  • ✅ Handle errors with try/except blocks
  • ✅ Use signals for external input

The add_worker method accepts:

app.add_worker(
